source.title_on_document: Voice-based debate with an AI adversary is associated with increased divergent ideation

supplement.where: Supporting Information, pp. 10-16 of this PDF, referred to as the SI Appendix in the main text (pp. 3, 4 and 6).
supplement.holds: Sample preprocessing and participant exclusions; conversation and voice-gender counts; pooled descriptive statistics and modality-switching checks (p. 10); text preprocessing and measure construction (pp. 11-12); a lexical-diversity word-count-control coefficient absent from Table 1 (p. 11); statistical-analysis details and two illustrative full transcripts (pp. 12-16). Main modality coefficients and clustered SEs are already in Table 1 (p. 9). Neither the main table nor this appendix provides outcome-specific statistics for the randomized voice-gender comparison.

paper_design_summary: MBA and EMBA students debated business strategy cases with the CAiSEY AI adversary, choosing voice or text for each interaction; the main analysis compares 957 analyzed conversations from 203 analyzed students using user and case fixed effects (pp. 2-3, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information). Computed scores on user-only text measure originality relative to the case reading, verbosity, repetition, and semantic breadth within each conversation (pp. 9, 11-12). AI voice gender was randomly assigned within spoken interactions, but its allocation procedure across repeated users is unspecified and its outcome results are reported only as a general statement of no effects (pp. 3, 5 and 10).

studies.label: CAiSEY business-case debates: self-selected communication modality with a nested randomized voice-gender comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: For the principal voice-versus-text contrast, students selected their modality for each CAiSEY interaction; neither modality nor its order was randomized (pp. 3 and 10). Session denotes the occasion of this choice. The analysis is an incomplete within-student panel: 186 of 203 analyzed users used both modalities, and the regressions include user and case fixed effects (pp. 3 and 9). The within code describes repeated modality observations, not randomized order. When students selected voice, perceived female versus male AI voice was randomly assigned (pp. 3 and 10). The no code refers only to modality; the nested randomization is retained in the arms and outcome contrasts. Neither the main text nor Supporting Information states whether voice gender was fixed by participant or reassigned across that participant’s spoken sessions, or explicitly establishes randomized voice-gender order for repeated users (pp. 3, 5 and 10-16). Thus a qualifying between-person allocation or randomized within-person order cannot be confirmed for the nested contrast.
assignment.quote: Users chose voice versus text for each CAiSEY interaction rather than being randomly assigned.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Supporting Information, Modality Switching Across Successive CAiSEY Sessions; p. 3, Approach (within-student modality overlap and nested voice-gender randomization); p. 9, Table 1 notes (user and case fixed effects)

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY (Walk-and-Talk; both voice genders)
arms.description: Students chose spoken debate with CAiSEY. There are 458 analyzed conversations, not 458 people; exact distinct people in this modality are not reported (p. 10, Descriptive Statistics). This parent condition includes both nested voice-gender conditions.

arms.name: Text-based CAiSEY
arms.description: Students chose typed debate with the same AI adversary, case readings, prompts, and opposition strategy (p. 3). There are 499 analyzed conversations, not 499 people; exact distinct people in this modality are not reported (p. 10).

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY: female voice (nested condition)
arms.description: Randomly assigned perceived female AI voice within the spoken condition; 240 analyzed conversations, not a reported count of distinct people. Nested within the voice parent condition and not an additional independent arm/sample (pp. 3 and 10).

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY: male voice (nested condition)
arms.description: Randomly assigned perceived male AI voice within the spoken condition; 218 analyzed conversations, not a reported count of distinct people. Nested within the voice parent condition and not an additional independent arm/sample (pp. 3 and 10).

participants.exclusions: The initial dataset included 224 students. Excluded 17 students who did not use CAiSEY in either the voice or text modalities required for the study, then 4 who lacked sufficient data for the word-count-adjusted lexical and semantic diversity measures; 203 students were analyzed (p. 10, Sample Preprocessing). These are not reported randomized-cohort counts. Distinct people analyzed separately by modality or voice gender are not reported.
participants.who: MBA and EMBA students in an elective Technology Strategy course at a U.S. business school (p. 2, Approach); the acknowledgments identify Columbia Business School (p. 6). The paper reports that 186 of 203 analyzed users used both modalities (p. 3). This establishes a lower bound of 186 distinct analyzed people contributing to the voice subset, whose conversations were assigned male or female AI voices (p. 10); it does not supply exact distinct-person counts by voice gender.
participants.quote: The analytic sample consists of 957 independent CAiSEY conversations generated by 203 MBA and EMBA students across 16 case-based assignments.
participants.locator: p. 10, Sample Preprocessing and Descriptive Statistics; p. 2, Approach, for U.S. course setting; p. 6, Acknowledgments. The paper calls conversations independent in this quote, but its regression SEs are clustered by user and case (pp. 9 and 12).

ai_tool.name_model: CAiSEY (Classroom Artificial Intelligence Studio for Engaging You); underlying generative model/version not stated (pp. 2-3, Approach).
ai_tool.how_used: In-house AI debate opponent. A student selected a position and gave an opening argument; CAiSEY automatically argued the opposite position and responded to the student in an extended exchange, through voice or text. It supplied counterarguments/content, so it is not coded as a content-free coach. It remained available while all scored user messages were produced (p. 3, Approach; pp. 12-16, example transcripts).

task.description: Generate and develop arguments and strategic proposals in open-ended debate about assigned business cases. Students read case background, chose a stance, and defended it against the AI interlocutor; for example, which content strategy Netflix should prioritize. The course offered 16 case readings, and AI use for each was optional (pp. 2-3, Approach). The paper explicitly describes debate as having no right answer and benefiting from different arguments (p. 2).
task.duration: Optional interactions over a course term spanning 16 case-based assignments; per-conversation duration or time limit not stated (p. 2, Approach; p. 10, Descriptive Statistics).

outcomes.name: Divergent ideation: within-conversation semantic diversity (word-count adjusted; raw variant retained)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: All text measures use concatenated user messages only, excluding AI messages (p. 11, Text Extraction). One analysis observation is one conversation, with repeated conversations per student; the analytic sample contains 957 analyzed conversations from 203 analyzed students (p. 10, Descriptive Statistics). Table 1 uses OLS with user and case fixed effects and standard errors clustered by user and case (pp. 9 and 12, Statistical Analyses). The paper operationalizes breadth of a single user's ideas, not diversity across different people. Cleaned user text is split into overlapping 50-word chunks with a 25-word step (50% overlap); all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encodes each chunk into 384 dimensions. Pairwise chunk cosine similarities, excluding the diagonal, are clipped to [0, 1], normalized to probabilities, and summarized using Shannon entropy. This compares chunks within one conversation. The primary score residualizes semantic diversity with respect to word count using user and case fixed effects; raw semantic diversity is retained as a variant in this same outcome (pp. 11-12, Divergent Ideation; p. 9, Models 9-10). The paper reports raw semantic diversity correlated with word count at r = 0.943 (p. 12). Coding flexibility reflects the codebook's distinction between within-person ideational variety and across-person diversity; this is an embedding-based proxy, not a count of idea categories. Figure 1 also uses conversation-level Welch two-sample t-tests, without a reported participant-clustered correction for those figure tests (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: Word-count-adjusted semantic diversity, Model 10: coefficient 0.178***, clustered SE (0.032); *** p<0.001. Raw semantic diversity, Model 9: coefficient 1.4***, clustered SE (0.058); *** p<0.001. Figure 1 marks the adjusted measure *** (p<0.001). These are voice-minus-text associations, not randomized modality effects. The two illustrative transcripts have semantic diversity = 4.51 (text) and 5.82 (voice); these are individual examples, not arm means. Analysis observations are conversations: voice N = 458 and text N = 499 (p. 10), not distinct people.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Table 1, Models 9-10 and notes; p. 8, Figure 1; p. 4, Findings; p. 5, representative-interaction discussion; p. 10, Descriptive Statistics (conversation Ns)

contrasts.reported: For the randomized voice-gender comparison, the paper states: "we find no evidence that AI persona affects any outcome variable." No outcome-specific coefficient, standard error, test statistic, p value, arm mean, or analyzed participant count is given. Female and male are labels for the two compared configurations; the paper designates neither as treatment or default control. This is a nested comparison within the spoken conversations, not a second independent sample.

outcomes.name: Within-conversation lexical diversity (word-count adjusted; raw and control-variable variants retained)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: All text measures use concatenated user messages only, excluding AI messages (p. 11, Text Extraction). One analysis observation is one conversation, with repeated conversations per student; the analytic sample contains 957 analyzed conversations from 203 analyzed students (p. 10, Descriptive Statistics). Table 1 uses OLS with user and case fixed effects and standard errors clustered by user and case (pp. 9 and 12, Statistical Analyses). Shannon entropy of the word-frequency distribution measures lexical repetition within a user's conversation. The paper names word-count-residualized lexical diversity as its primary repetition outcome; residualization uses user and case fixed effects. Unadjusted entropy and the specification including word count as a covariate are variants of this same outcome. Raw lexical diversity correlates with word count at r = 0.801 (p. 11, Repetition). It is not similarity between different people's outputs, so it is coded other/with_ai. Direction below follows the primary adjusted specification; the raw specification has the opposite sign. Figure 1 uses conversation-level Welch tests (p. 8). The direction field follows the explicitly designated primary adjusted measure; the opposite raw association remains in reported. This is a choice of the primary specification, not a claim that all variants have the same sign.

contrasts.reported: Word-count-adjusted lexical diversity, Model 8: coefficient -0.042*, clustered SE (0.018); * p<0.05. Raw lexical diversity, Model 7: coefficient 0.262***, clustered SE (0.023); *** p<0.001. The appendix reports a word-count-control specification as beta = -0.105, p < 0.001 and describes it as substantively identical/equivalent; it supplies no SE for that coefficient. Figure 1 marks the adjusted measure *** (p<0.001), based on Welch tests rather than Table 1's fixed-effects regressions. The appendix coefficient and Table 1 coefficient are preserved separately as printed. Analysis observations are conversations: voice N = 458 and text N = 499 (p. 10), not distinct people.

eligibility.reason: The principal voice-versus-text comparison fails criterion 1 because modality was self-selected for each interaction (pp. 3 and 10); its numerical coefficients remain observational. A nested female-versus-male AI voice comparison is explicitly described as randomized (pp. 3 and 10), but the document does not establish whether allocation was fixed by person or repeated across sessions, or whether within-person condition order was randomized. Criterion 1 and paper-level core eligibility therefore remain unclear pending the voice-gender allocation procedure. Criterion 2 is met: 203 students were analyzed after exclusions (p. 10), and 186 of those analyzed users used both modalities (p. 3), establishing at least 186 distinct people in the analyzed voice subset. All analyzed voice conversations are assigned one of the two voice genders (p. 10). This lower bound supports the 50-person threshold without treating conversation counts as people or inventing exact gender-arm counts. Criterion 3 is met because originality and within-conversation ideational breadth were computed on student-only output (pp. 11-12), produced during responsive debate with generative AI (pp. 2-3); the paper also states that the randomized voice-gender analysis found no evidence of effects on any outcome (p. 5). Missing outcome-specific gender estimates affect extraction, not the existence of qualifying output measures. All retained outcomes answer with_ai; none measures similarity across people or performance after AI removal.

one_line_finding: Among 203 analyzed students, self-selected voice rather than text debate with CAiSEY was associated with greater word-count-adjusted within-conversation semantic breadth (coefficient 0.178, clustered SE 0.032, p < 0.001; p. 9, Table 1, Model 10; participant count p. 10).
open_questions: For the nested randomized voice-gender comparison, was voice gender assigned once per person or reassigned across spoken sessions, and was condition order randomized for users exposed to both voices? The PDF does not specify this procedure (pp. 3, 5 and 10-16). Author clarification is needed for criterion 1; core eligibility remains unclear.

What are the exact distinct-person counts analyzed in each modality and voice-gender condition? These remain unreported; participant-linked analysis data would settle them. This does not prevent criterion 2 from being met: 203 people were analyzed, and 186 used both modalities, establishing at least 186 in the analyzed voice subset (pp. 3 and 10).

What are the outcome-specific estimates, uncertainty and analysis specifications for the randomized voice-gender comparison? The source supplies only a general no-evidence statement (p. 5). Authors could provide these extraction details; they do not change the confirmed presence of output-scored outcomes.

Why does the appendix describe the lexical-diversity word-count-control result as equivalent/substantively identical while reporting beta = -0.105, p < 0.001 (p. 11), versus -0.042 (SE 0.018), p < 0.05 in Table 1 Model 8 (p. 9)? Author clarification would settle the discrepancy; both specifications remain as printed, and it does not affect eligibility.

Which underlying generative model/version powered CAiSEY? The PDF does not name it (pp. 1-3). Author clarification would improve tool identification; the described generative AI interaction already establishes its scope.

Where are the anonymized data and replication code that p. 6 says are available? No repository URL is printed, and the p. 12 CAiSEY link is a demonstration. Authors could provide the URLs; their absence does not independently affect eligibility.

What is the date and version identifier of the exact manuscript on file? The PDF does not print them (p. 1). Authors could identify this version; this provenance gap does not affect the three eligibility criteria.
notes: The unchanged reconciliation object records the earlier comparison of both raw screening forms. Read the entire 44,000-character markdown conversion, including all supporting information and representative transcripts. Source PDF pages were extracted for every recorded numerical result and eligibility fact; Table 1 was also checked with table extraction and Figure 1 was inspected directly from an in-memory rendering. Eight output measures are retained; ten table columns reduce to eight outcomes by grouping raw/adjusted variants. Outcome order follows B; the matched A-to-final IDs are O1=O1, O2=O2, O3=O3, O4=O4, O5=O8, O6=O5, O7=O6, O8=O7. Ordering, synonymous arm labels, equivalent prose, and empty synthesis defaults are not counted as substantive differences. All requested comparison categories were reviewed: design, assignment, arms, people counts, AI tool/role, task, outcome inventory and attributes, statistics/locators, supplement, overlap, company role, each eligibility criterion, and main finding. The differences list separates additional printed statistics from coding disagreements; there is no outcome unique to one screener. Observational is used because both self-selected conditions used AI and the form defines quasi_people in terms of work with and without AI. Assignment unit session denotes the occasion of modality choice; structure within describes the repeated student panel despite incomplete use of both modalities. No between-person assigned factor for modality is reported. One dataset is represented; the voice-gender subconditions are nested, not additional independent samples. Exact arm-specific people counts remain null. Table 1 calls its modality Ns users, whereas Figure 1 and p. 10 explicitly identify them as conversations. N_units is the overall conversation count; the gender contrasts use the voice subset. All text measures use user-only contributions. Semantic breadth compares chunks within a conversation and is flexibility; lexical repetition is other. No across_people or after_ai outcome is reported. Message count measures elaboration, not idea fluency. The finalizer corrected the measure codes for message count and total word count to null: neither has a fitting code under the current measure vocabulary. Definitions, elaboration constructs and reported statistics remain intact; these null codes do not affect criterion 3. For lexical diversity, the direction field follows the explicitly primary adjusted result; the positive raw coefficient and the differing appendix coefficient are retained. Figure 1 uses conversation-level Welch tests; Table 1 instead uses user/case fixed effects and standard errors clustered by user and case. Figure significance marks, pooled descriptives and individual illustrative transcripts are identified separately from arm estimates. Gender null directions come only from the paper-wide qualitative statement; no outcome-specific estimate is invented. Female/male ordering is administrative. No effect sizes, confidence intervals, or arm-level people counts were computed. Page 6 asserts data/code availability without a repository URL; https://caisey.me/demo on p. 12 is a demonstration, not a repository. Reconciliation n_unresolved counts unresolved differences between the forms; remaining reporting gaps shared by both forms are retained in open_questions and eligibility, and do not become artificial disagreements. Final review read all 330 markdown lines and extracted all 16 PDF pages, checked Table 1 with find_tables, and inspected Figure 1 in memory. The three challenge files contain three problems: two outcome-code problems were corrected and the assignment-procedure problem remains open. No people-count problem was raised. The 186 analyzed users who used both modalities establish a lower bound for the voice subset, so exact gender-arm counts are not an eligibility blocker. The sole open eligibility issue is qualifying voice-gender allocation/order across repeated users. All existing reconciliation differences have status resolved; the reconciliation object is unchanged. Final n_corrected/n_rejected/n_open count challenge problems, while final.open_items separately classifies reporting gaps.

open_items.item: Voice-gender allocation across repeated users: fixed assignment by person versus repeated session allocation, and randomized condition order if users experienced both voices. The PDF states random assignment but supplies no such procedure (pp. 3, 5 and 10-16). Author confirmation of a qualifying between-person allocation or randomized within-person order would settle criterion 1 and core eligibility.

Exact distinct-person counts analyzed by modality and voice gender (open_questions and the unconfirmed reconciliation eligibility entry). Participant-linked analysis data would provide these counts. Criterion 2 is already met: 203 analyzed students and 186 users of both modalities establish at least 186 distinct people in the analyzed voice subset (pp. 3 and 10); conversation counts remain separate.

Outcome-specific voice-gender estimates, uncertainty and analysis specifications beyond the general no-evidence statement (p. 5). Authors could provide the missing results; their absence does not negate output scoring under criterion 3.

Lexical-diversity specification discrepancy: appendix beta = -0.105, p < 0.001 (p. 11) versus Table 1 Model 8 coefficient -0.042, SE 0.018, p < 0.05 (p. 9), despite the claimed equivalence. Authors could identify a specification difference or correct a reporting error. Both printed results are retained; no eligibility criterion depends on their magnitude or significance.
Underlying CAiSEY generative model/version is unreported (pp. 1-3). Authors could identify it; the described system already establishes use of generative AI.

Data and replication-code repository URLs are absent despite the availability statement (p. 6); the p. 12 link is a live demonstration. Authors could supply the access locations. This access gap is not an additional eligibility criterion.
Date/version identifier for the saved manuscript is absent from the PDF (p. 1). Authors could identify the exact version; this provenance gap does not affect eligibility.
